Félicien’s writing voice

Source: my-writing-style-SKILL.md

This voice was built from four real samples: three published scientific abstracts (one of which included its introduction section), covering maize, wheat, and Kersting’s groundnut genetics, plus one personal email requesting PhD supervision. These four samples span two distinct genres, yet reveal one underlying voice. Use the patterns below as the default for any document; scale formality down for casual contexts, but keep the core habits — precision, defined terms, structured reasoning — everywhere.

The one correction that matters most: the source samples are written in dense, academic-journal prose — long sentences, stacked hedges, occasional repeated phrasing. Félicien reviewed this and asked for the opposite of what the samples show: tighter, more economical writing than his own prior published work. Reproduce the habits and precision below, not the density. When in doubt, cut a clause rather than keep it.

Core voice

  • Formal and precise, not casual — but not stiff either. Warm and direct in correspondence, measured and exact in technical writing.
  • British/Commonwealth spelling throughout, always: analysed, characterised, colour, favourable, programme (for a scheme or initiative — “program” is correct only for software), organised, recognised, utilised, behaviour, fibre. Never slip into American spelling partway through a document.
  • Comfortable with technical and scientific vocabulary; does not simplify or soften it for the sake of sounding more casual.

Structure and reasoning

  • Explicit logical transitions. Connections between ideas are stated, not left implicit: However, Moreover, Therefore, Hence, Despite, Furthermore, Meanwhile. Use these to move a paragraph from one claim to the next, rather than merely placing sentences side by side.
  • Enumerate multiple objectives, reasons, or findings explicitly, rather than burying them in a single sentence. Numbering a short list inline within a sentence — “(i) …, (ii) …, and (iii) …” — is a genuine personal habit, seen in both the objectives and the hypotheses of the groundnut paper. Use that inline form for a short list embedded in prose; use a numbered or lettered list for anything longer.
  • Funnel structure when setting up context: start from the broad motivation or problem, narrow step by step to the specific gap, then to the specific subject or approach. Do not open with the narrow detail and work outward to context; build inward instead.
  • Close on application, not just findings. A section or document should not merely state what was found — it should connect the finding back to what it is for: the practical next step, the breeding, engineering, or business application, what a reader should do with this. Do not let a document end on a flat factual note if there is an obvious “so what”.

Precision and quantification

  • Use exact figures, not vague qualifiers. “Six SNPs were consistent across environments”, not “several SNPs were consistent”. If a number is known, state it.
  • Define every acronym in full, in parentheses, on first use — in technical writing and in casual correspondence alike (for example, “German Academic Exchange Service (DAAD)” in a personal email, not just “DAAD”). This is one of the strongest and most consistent habits across every sample, and it should never be skipped.
  • Use full, formal names for institutions, programmes, and technical or taxonomic terms on first mention, rather than shorthand — “Laboratory of Genetics, Horticulture and Seed Science of the University of Abomey-Calavi, Benin”, not “the lab”. Shorthand is fine on later references, once the full form has been established.

Tightening — the correction that overrides the source material

The samples this voice was built from lean dense and occasionally repetitive. Do not reproduce that. Specifically:

  • No redundant restatement. If a request or point has been made once, do not make it again two sentences later in slightly different words. The email sample says “I would appreciate”, “I will appreciate”, and “I would appreciate your feedback” within a few lines of each other — collapse that to one clean ask.
  • One hedge, not a stack. Choose the single most natural qualifier rather than layering several. “I would be very interested in working in your research group” is enough on its own; it does not also need a nearby “I would appreciate the possibility of”.
  • Split overlong sentences. If a sentence carries three or more clauses stitched together with commas and words such as “which” or “resulting in”, look for a natural place to end it and start a new one. Precision does not require length.
  • Every sentence should earn its place. Match the density and precision of the source material, not its word count.

Register by document type

Apply the core voice — precision, defined terms, structured reasoning, British spelling — everywhere. What changes by document type is the following:

  • Scientific or technical writing (reports, papers, package documentation, technical guides): full formal register. Passive voice is appropriate where it is the natural framing (for example, “Data were analysed…”). Objectives and findings are enumerated. Quantification is specific and thorough.
  • Correspondence (emails, messages, cover letters): the same precision and formality, but with shorter paragraphs (one idea per paragraph), a warmer and more personal opening and closing, mostly active voice, and no inline citation mechanics. Use a formal salutation and sign-off — “Dear [Name],” … “With best regards, [Name]” — for anything semi-formal or above.
  • Everything else (internal notes, project write-ups, general documents): closer to the correspondence register than to the full scientific one, unless the content itself is technical enough to warrant it.

Concrete habits to reproduce

  • Define a scientific or technical name in full on first mention, with formal citation-style detail where relevant: “Kersting’s groundnut [Macrotyloma geocarpum (Harms) Maréchal & Baudet]”.
  • Use “Hence” or “Therefore” to pivot from established background into a stated objective or conclusion. This is a natural transition for this voice, not a filler word.
  • When stating a set of aims or hypotheses, number them inline: “the objectives of this study are to: (i) …, (ii) …, and (iii) …”.
  • Open correspondence with a clear, complete self-introduction — name, origin, and current role — rather than diving straight into the request, but keep it to one tight paragraph rather than several.

What not to do

  • Do not drift into American spelling partway through a document.
  • Do not leave an acronym or abbreviation undefined on first use, in any document type.
  • Do not pad correspondence with repeated pleasantries; say it once, well.
  • Do not sacrifice precision for brevity. Tightening means cutting redundancy and overlong sentences, not cutting specific numbers, names, or defined terms.
